list.listitem: Bacterial Vaginosis (BV), Vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) and trichomoniasis are the most common causes of vulvovaginitis (VV). Microscopy of the vaginal discharge (wet mount) or laboratory testing with nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) or culturecan assist in determining an etiology for vaginitis. A

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) guidelines (2020) recommend use of Amsel clinical criteria or Gram stain with Nugent scoring for the diagnosis of BV and NAA testing for the diagnosis of trichomoniasis. A
Avoid empiric therapy for any vulvovaginitis. C
Metronidazole is first-line treatment for BV and trichomoniasis. A
Intravaginal and oral antifungals are equally efficacious for VVC. A

Follow-up and test of cure (TOC) for most cases of vaginitis are not required if symptoms resolve. C However, due to high recurrence rates for trichomoniasis, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC, 2021) and ACOG (2020) recommend retesting within 3 months post treatment. B
Pap tests are not reliable for the diagnosis of VV. B

background.definition: Vaginitis is defined as an inflammatory response of vaginal and vulvar mucosa either from an infectious or noninfectious source that is associated with a spectrum of symptoms including abnormal vaginal discharge, burning, odor, itching, irritation, dyspareunia and vulvovaginal discomfort.

list.listitem: Most common is BV followed by VVC. True incidence is unknown as vulvovaginitis including BV, VVC and trichomoniasis are NOT reportable. Differs across countries and populations; variations are noted based on age, hormonal status, and sexual activity. Reproductive age group along with hormonal changes, pregnancy and menopause can have a higher impact on incidence.

Based on an online survey, the annual incidence of self-reported healthcare provider diagnosed VVC was 5.2% and recurrent VVC among those with VVC was 4.7% and was similar for United Sates (US) and European patients.

Globally, BV is the most common cause of vaginal discharge among women of reproductive age, with an estimated prevalence ranging from 23% to 29%. Based on a study among reproductive-aged women in the U.S., 21.2 million (29.2%) had BV, of whom about 84% were asymptomatic. The estimated prevalence was 51.4% among African-Americans (AA), 32% among Mexican-Americans, and 23% among non-Hispanic whites.

BV prevalence increases with number of sexual partners and with partner concurrency. BV among sexually-inactive women was 18.8%, pregnant women 25%, and women who have ever been pregnant 31.7%. A study including 14,193 French women, estimated 7.1% to 16% had BV during pregnancy.

Trichomoniasis affects approximately 2.6 million persons in the U.S. A U.S. study among reproductive-age women estimated prevalence of trichomoniasis of 3.1 % for patients between age 14 years to 49 years, with an ethnic distribution, in descending order, of AA 13.3%, Hispanic 1.8%, and Caucasian 1.3%.

The most recent data from the CDC showed a prevalence rate of T. vaginalis of 2.1% among U.S. females and 0.5% among males. The highest rates are among Black females (9.6%) and Black males (3.6%), compared with non-Hispanic White women (0.8%) and Hispanic women (1.4%).

Trichomoniasis has a four times higher rate of infection among symptomatic vs. asymptomatic women (26% versus 6.5%). Prevalence rates are increased with incarceration and with concomitant BV infection. Among 276 adolescents presenting to a pediatric emergency department with lower abdominal or genitourinary symptoms, the prevalence of Trichomonas vaginalis was 9.9% (95% CI, 5.7%-14.0%).

VVC is considered the second most common cause of vaginitis after BV. VVC affects up to 75% of women of childbearing age at least once in their life time. Half of initially-infected women may have a second episode, and up to 5% to 10% of women experience recurrent VVC (defined as more than three episodes annually).

Recurrent VVC global prevalence was estimated to be 3871 per 100,000 women, with 9% among the 25 to 34-year age group. The global burden of recurrent VVC is about 138 million women annually, predicted to increase to 150 million by 2030. Approximately 40% of females may experience VVC and 8% may have recurrent VVC by age 50 years; this varied widely by country (from 23% to 49%) as did the estimated probability of recurrent VVC (from 14% to 28%,).

A Taiwan study identified prevalence of trichomoniasis, BV, and VVC of 2.1%, 22.8%, and 21.7%, respectively. Coinfections of BV and VVC, trichomoniasis and BV, trichomoniasis and VVC, and triple infection were noted to be 5.0%, 0.2%, 0.2%, and 0.7%, respectively.
In a UK population study of women seeking care in an urban sexual health clinic (2004-2008), the prevalence of non-albicans yeasts remained stable at between 0.87% and 1.06%.

The estimated annual global economic burden of treating symptomatic BV is US $4.8 (95% CI, $3.7-$6.1) billion and, in the US, the economic burden tripled when including costs of BV-associated preterm births and human immunodeficiency virus cases.

Annually, VVC accounts for approximately 1,354,331 outpatient visits and $368 million on treatment and missed time from work. The projected economic burden of recurrent VVC due to lost productivity could be up to US $14 billion to $39 billion annually.

Pelvic inflammatory disease, endometritis, or vaginal cuff cellulitis can rarely occur from BV after invasive procedures. Women with BV have an increased relative risk of chlamydia (2.3), gonorrhea (1.2), HPV 1.2, and trichomoniasis (2.9, adjusted OR 1.9, 95% CI 1.4-2.4).

Among pregnant women, BV is associated with low-birth-weight, preterm delivery of a low-birth-weight infant (but not preterm delivery overall), and clinical chorioamnionitis. Data are conflicting as to whether BV is associated with an increased risk of preterm labor.
There is a weak positive association between BV and cervical pre-cancerous lesions (overall estimated odds ratio 1.5, 95% CI 1.2-1.8).

BV is associated with an increased risk of HIV-1 acquisition in women and from women infected with HIV to their uninfected male partners; in one study of 2236 HIV-infected African women, the incidence in men whose HIV-1-infected partner had BV was 2.9 versus 0.76 per 100 person-years in men whose female partner had normal vaginal flora (hazard ratio 3.6, 95% CI 1.7-7.5).

According to CDC T. vaginalis infection is associated with a 1.5 -fold increased risk for HIV acquisition, 1.4 x times greater likelihood of preterm birth, premature rupture of membranes, and infants who are small for gestational age.
A meta-analysis has shown an association between trichomniasis and a 2-fold increase risk for cervical cancer.

The frequency of specific causes varies somewhat with the population studied. For example, trichomonas is more common in younger women with multiple partners, and atrophic vaginitis is more common in postmenopausal women. A case-control study suggested that oral sex may be a risk factor for vvc; increased frequency and number of sexual partners, early age at first intercourse, recent antibiotic use, oral contraceptives, and tight clothing were not identified as risk factors.

BV: 15% to 50%; a change in the balance of vaginal bacteria. BV is a polymicrobial vaginal dysbiosis (a poly-microbial clinical syndrome resulting from replacement of the normal hydrogen peroxide producing Lactobacillus sp. in the vagina with high concentrations of anaerobic bacteria, Gardnerella vaginalis, Ureaplasma, Mycoplasma, and other anaerobes).,,
Trichomoniasis: 5% to 50%.

Aerobic vaginosis: 4% to 7%, caused by Group B streptococcus, Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, Enterococcus fecalis. In a recent study of pathogenic vaginal bacteria (streptococcus, staphylococcus, enterococcus, escherichia/shigella, haemophilus, and campylobacter) in women from Africa and the Netherlands, 17% contained a relative abundance of at least 1%.
Lactobacillosis: 15%, normal vaginal flora lactobacilli of length 5-15 µm becomes pathogenic when it is extremely long lactobacilli 40 and 75 µm of length.
Bacterial Vaginitis: No particular bacteria except for Group A Streptococcus, no casual relationship has been established.
Atrophic vaginitis (genitourinary syndrome of menopause (see Menopause chapter).

listitem.strong: Allergic/contact dermatitis: Contact irritation or allergic reaction. Infrequent, non infection and inflammatory.

list.listitem: Foreign body

Healthy vaginal flora is comprised of approximately 90% lactobacilli, contributing to a vaginal pH of 3.8-4.2 normally, maintaining homeostasis. Vaginitis occurs when the vaginal flora and the vaginal environment become altered or by introduction of pathogenic organisms. Vaginal environment can be altered due to changes in estrogen or progesterone levels, sexual intercourse, douching, stress, and use of antibiotics or contraceptives.

Elevation of the vaginal pH (normal pH 3.8-4.2) due to a reduction in hydrogen peroxide and lactic acid producing Lactobacillus acidophilus (normal vaginal flora) can result in bacterial overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria, including G. vaginalis, Prevotella species, Mobiluncus species, and A. vaginae, which can also increase the virulence of Trichomonas vaginalis.

Estrogen increases glycogen content in vaginal epithelial cells which encourages lactobacilli colonization, increasing lactic acid production and decreasing vaginal pH; this protects against growth of pathogenic organisms. Changes in estrogen and progesterone levels enhance the virulence of trichomonas vaginitis and increase adherence of candida. Increased glycogen production during pregnancy facilitates adherence of candida to the vaginal epithelium.

Likewise, alkalinization of the vagina from frequent unprotected intercourse may enhance a shift from lactobacilli-dominated microflora to BV-like microflora; in addition, transfer of perineal bacteria may be another pathogenic factor for BV.

In one longitudinal study of 71 women, onset of sexual intercourse was not associated with a change in vaginal colonization with Lactobacillus species for most women, although colonization with Gardnerella vaginalis increased somewhat (56% vs 39%).

Pubertal status appears to influence the organisms associated with vulvovaginitis; in a study of 112 girls, 38/72 pre pubertal girls with this diagnosis had a positive vaginal culture, most commonly group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus (15.2%), while 19/40 pubertal girls with vulvovaginitis had a positive vaginal culture, most commonly Candida albicans (27.5%).
New data suggest that local mucosal overreaction of the immune system rather than a defective host response to Candida colonization is responsible for VVC.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Intra vaginal insertion of over-the-counter products (VCC)

list.listitem: There is no evidence to support routine screening of pregnant women for BV, and the USPSTF (2020) recommends against screening for BV among pregnant women who are not at increased risk of preterm delivery. There are insufficient data to determine benefits and harms of screening for BV among pregnant persons who are at increased risk for preterm delivery. A

However, in a phase 2 trial of 228 women with prior BV who underwent randomization (152 to Lactin-V [Lactobacillus crispatus CTV-05] and 76 to placebo administered vaginally over 11 weeks), women in the Lactin-V group had significantly lower incidence of BV recurrence at 12 weeks (30% vs 45%, respectively).

In one study of 4155 pregnant women who were screened and treated before 20 weeks gestation for BV, trichomoniasis and VVC, there were lower rates of preterm delivery and preterm low-birth-weight infants than for control women (3% vs 5%).
To prevent reinfection with trichomoniasis, partners need to be treated. A
Use of a male or female latex condom prevents trichomoniasis; nonoxynol-9 does not prevent trichomoniasis, VVC or BV. A
The probiotic Lactobacillus used during antibiotic therapy does not prevent post-antibiotic VVC. A

There are insufficient data to recommend Lactobacillus, yogurt, garlic, tea tree oil, low-carbohydrate diet, candida desensitization, hormone therapy, or douching for prevention of candidiasis or BV. B

The initial thorough evaluation consists of a history, physical examination, and testing of vaginal discharge for appropriate diagnosis. Test by wet mount slide in office for identifying probable cause by pH testing, potassium hydroxide (10%)-whiff's test and microscopic exam using 0.9% saline or use commercially available US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-cleared NAAT for diagnosing vaginitis; consider vaginal culture.
ACOG guidelines (2020) recommend use of Amsel clinical criteria 3/4 or Gram stain with Nugent scoring 7/10 for the diagnosis of BV and NAAT for the diagnosis of trichomoniasis. C.
Fishy odor is more consistent with BV, foul or fishy smell with trichomoniasis, and odorless with VVC. C
Thick curdy discharge, vulvar fissures, or erythema with symptoms of burning or itching suggest VVC. C
Lactobacillosis produces variable discharge and cyclical symptoms occurring during the luteal phase. B

Diagnosis, per expert opinion of the ACOG (2020), is based on the following either alone or in combination: Medical history and physical exam of the vulva and vagina, speculum examination, and clinical testing of vaginal discharge using Amsel's criteria 3/4: (homogenous thin white/grey discharge, pH >4.5 on vaginal fluid, 10% potassium hydroxide “whiff test” and >20% clue cells vaginal smear under microscopy) or NAAT. Trichomoniasis is diagnosed by observing motile trichomonads under microscopy, vaginal pH>4.5, and strawberry cervix; or NAAT. Whiff test may or may not be positive with trichomoniasis. Candiasis is diagnosed by curdy, white, cottage-cheese-like discharge; normal vaginal pH of 4 to 4.5; and microscopy positive for fungal hyphae or pseudo hyphae with 10% potassium hydroxide; or NAAT or vaginal culture.

Reported Amsel clinical criteria sensitivity of 92% and a specificity of 77% compared with Gram stain with Nugent scoring. Commercial multiplex PCR panel may be an option when office microscope is not available to detect common causes of vaginitis: BV, VVC and trichomoniasis.

Identify the type, duration, and timing of the discharge and typical symptoms of vaginitis (e.g., itching, burning, fishy odor, or dysuria). Also identify risk factors for vaginitis: sexual activity, sexual abuse, medications (e.g., steroids, oral contraceptives, and antibiotics), diabetes mellitus, and immunocompromise.

Perform a vaginal examination and take a sample of vaginal secretions. A speculum examination is not routinely necessary.If cervical motion tenderness, fever, dyspareunia, and cervical/vaginal discharge are present, consider pelvic inflammatory disease.
BV: Asymptomatic 50% of the time; absence of fishy odor and/or itching reduces the likelihood of BV and is more consistent with vaginal candidiasis.
Trichomoniasis: Burning and itching best rule in trichomoniasis, while absence of introital discharge, foul/fishy odor, or inflamed (strawberry) cervix best rule it out.

Candida: Findings that best increase the likelihood of candida are thick, curdy vaginal discharge; vulvar edema or fissures on examination; and a chief complaint of pruritus or burning. Absence of vulvar pruritus, pain/burning, swelling, and redness reduce the likelihood of candida, as does absence of vulvar erythema.

Aerobic vaginitis: Dyspareunia, burning, itching, purulent discharge, pH >4.5, occasional bleeding, foul smelling but not fishy odor or inflamed red, ecchymotic and superficial ulcerations of the cervix.
Lactobacillosis produces profuse and variable discharge and/ or cyclical symptoms occurring during the luteal phase.
Initial evaluation consists of thorough history and physical examination, and tests for specific infections and excluding sexually transmitted infections (STIs).

Wet mount and microscopic examination of the vaginal discharge is an ancillary test in the diagnosis of vulvovaginitis and adequate to establish the diagnosis., Collect the specimen using endocervical brush, a plastic spatula, or a Dacron swab without touching the cervix as it can identify false positive leukcocytes. Avoid using cotton swabs as the cotton fibers may interfere with the sample. However, based on a systematic review, about 30% (range 7% to 72%) of women with vaginal complaints go without a diagnosis even after a complete evaluation.

Pap tests are not considered reliable for diagnosis of vaginitis. Similarly, vaginal WBC counts of at least 11 WBCs/HPF are associated with increased odds of having gonorrhea, chlamydia, or trichomoniasis, but based on low sensitivity (48.2% to 53.9%) and specificity (67.2% to 68.8%) have limited diagnostic utility.

A wet mount with more than 20% clue cells and a positive whiff test are reasonably accurate, but the diagnosis is best supported by a combination of clue cells and amine odor (LR+ 12.6) or a pH of 4.5 or higher with an amine odor (LR+ 12.8) or clue cells (LR+ 8.6). Use of Amsel's criteria 3/4 (see Clinical decision rules section) has a high specificity with a positive likelihood ratio of 9.9. The best test to rule out the diagnosis is less than 20% clue cells or a pH less than 4.5. If more than 5 WBCs are seen per high powered field, chlamydia or gonorrhea is possible. The "FemExam Card" test is helpful if both pH and amine are positive (LR+ 8.0).
Gram stain (Nugent score 7-10 based on lactobacillus morphotypes, Gardenella/Bacteroides morphotypes and variable rods) is mostly used in research.

Rapid antigen testing by Gen-Probe or Aptima DNA probe test of the vaginal fluid for Gardenella vaginalis or detection of sialidase activity in vaginal fluid had a sensitivity of 92% to 100% and specificity of 92% to 98%.

ACOG (2020) notes that these tests can be used as alternatives to gram stain with Nugent scoring but that a single sentinel organism, as identified in the DNA probe, has not been found that accurately identifies patients with BV.
Commercially available FDA approved NAAT/PCR testing, particularly using the single-swab panel test that combines multiplex PCR and DNA probe technology, is comparable for diagnosing BV.
Self-testing for elevated pH or sialidase is reasonably specific (67% and 90%, respectively) compared to clinician diagnosis of BV.

A wet mount showing motile trichomonads and leukocytes rules in the diagnosis, sensitivity 58% to 82%. Leukorrhea alone, without demonstration of motile trichomonads, suggests trichomoniasis and requires additional testing.

ACOG guidelines (2020) recommend NAAT for the diagnosis of trichomoniasis. One such test, the Aptima T. vaginalis assay (Beckton Dickinson) is FDA cleared for detection of T. vaginalis from symptomatic or asymptomatic women.
Commercially available FDA approved NAAT can be performed on vaginal, cervical, or urine specimens with equal sensitivity (95.3%-100%) and specificity (95.2%-100%).

Several rapid tests are also FDA cleared for diagnosis including Solana trichomonas assay (Quidel) from female vaginal and urine specimens from asymptomatic and symptomatic women (sensitivity >98% vs. NAAT for vaginal specimens and >92% for urine specimens) and the Amplivue trichomonas assay (Quidel) for vaginal specimens from symptomatic and asymptomatic women (sensitivity 90.7% and specificity of 98.9%, vs. NAAT).

The Gen-Probe Aptima T. vaginalis transcription-mediated amplification assay was more sensitive than the BD Affirm VPIII hybridization assay in identifying trichomonas. In another study of women with HIV, PCR assay for the amplification of adhesion gene appeared to be more sensitive for trichomonas compared to culture. The OSOM Trichomonas Rapid Test, an antigen-detection immunochromatographic assay, has sensitivity of 97.98% and specificity 99.37%.
Self-testing with rapid point-of-care tests has high specificity (99.1%) and may be useful in management of TV.
Wet mount using 10% KOH and demonstrating fungal hyphae identify vulvovaginal candidiasis, sensitivity of 65% to 85%.

ACOG (2020) guidelines recommend diagnosis of VVC based on one of the following two findings: 1) visualization of spores, pseudohyphae, or hyphae on wet-mount microscopy or 2) vaginal fungal culture or commercial diagnostic test results positive for Candida species.
Yeast rapid antigen tests perform adequately, with a sensitivity of 73% and a specificity of 84%; however, with a negative predictive value of 82% such tests do not rule out candidiasis.

Self-testing (Savyon Diagnostics) in patients with recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis has a positive predictive value ranging between 92% to 100%, is less expensive, and may allow for earlier initiation of therapy.

An immunochromatography test, the CandiVagi assay (SR2B, Avrille, France), for rapid diagnosis of vulvovaginal candidiasis was more sensitive than microscopic examination (96.6% vs. 61%) with similar specificity (98.6% vs. 100%), and compared favorably with culture.
Culture is useful in diagnosing BV or VVC if wet mount is inconclusive.
Diagnosed by fresh wet mount microscopy with physiologic saline solution, greater than 50 lactobacilli present per field at a high-power magnification.
A wet mount showing parabasal cells, leukocytes, yellowish discharge, negative whiff test, few or no lactobacillus and immature epithelial cells.
Use rapid antigen testing (e.g., Gen-Probe, Aptima DNA probe test) or culture for diagnosing AV.

Amsel criteria are helpful for diagnosis of BV. They are: (1) thin homogeneous discharge, (2) positive whiff test, (3) clue cell under microscopy, and (4) vaginal pH greater than 4.5. Presence of at least 3 out of 4 criteria is strong evidence in favor of BV (LR+ 9.9).

VVC diagnosis, based on ACOG (2020) guidelines, is the presence of one of the following two findings: 1) visualization of spores, pseudo-hyphae, or hyphae on wet-mount microscopy or 2) vaginal fungal culture or commercial FDA-approved (NAAT) diagnostic test results positive for Candida species. VVC is classified as complicated if it is recurrent (4 or more episodes of candidiasis annually) or severe; is non-albicans candidiasis; or occurs in women with uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression, or in those who are pregnant.
See algorithm for diagnosis of vaginitis ().
Metronidazole is first-line treatment for BV in nonpregnant symptomatic women and for trichomoniasis; intravaginal treatment of BV is equally effective as oral therapy. A
Clindamycin can also be used as a first-line agent for BV, clindamycin and metronidazole are equally effective for eradicating symptoms of BV. A
Sexual partners of women with BV do not require treatment. C Sexual partners of women with trichomoniasis require treatment. A
Uncomplicated VVC is treated with antifungals: 3-day intravaginal or 1-day oral for nonpregnant women and 7 days of an intravaginal antifungal for pregnant women. A
Oral and vaginal antifungals are equally effective for the treatment of uncomplicated VVC. A
Lactobacillosis: treat with amoxicillin 500 mg twice a day for 7 days; if penicillin allergy can use doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. B
Atrophic vaginitis symptoms are well relieved by vaginal estrogen therapy. A
See for recommendations regarding drug treatment of vaginitis. Drug therapy is based on CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021.

Treat symptomatic nonpregnant or pregnant patients with metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days (92% cure rate and 13%-44% relapse rate) OR metronidazole gel 0.75%, 5g (one full applicator) daily intravaginally for 5 days OR clindamycin cream 2% 5g (one full applicator) daily intravaginally for 5 days or ovule (100 mg daily for 3 days), (87% cure rate and 0%-53% relapse rate). For nonpregnant patients, tinidazole 2 g orally once daily for 2 days OR tinidazole 1g orally once daily for 5 days OR secnidazole 2g orally in a single dose OR clindamycin 300 mg orally twice daily for 7 days OR clindamycin ovules 100 mg intravaginally once at bedtime for 3 days are also effective options for treatment of BV. Cure rates are identical to metronidazole irrespective of regimen but clindamycin tends to have a lower rate of adverse effects..
Although 6 RCTs have been performed on partner treatment, significant methodologic flaws prevent firm conclusions on BV outcomes; partner treatment is not currently recommended.

In 1 large RCT, single 2-g dose of secnidazole (a nitroimidazole related to metronidazole) was shown to be as effective as the multiple-dose metronidazole regimen for BV (60.1% cured women vs. 59.5%).

In a recent meta-analysis of 6 studies, authors concluded that there was no difference between oral secnidazole and metronidazole, but that ornidazole was superior to single-dose oral secnidazole in clinical cure at the 4th week after treatment (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.73- 0.89).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 4 studies found greater microbiological cure of BV with an oral metronidazole/probiotic regimen (OR 0.09; 95% CI, 0.03-0.26) or probiotic/estriol preparation (OR 0.02; 95% CI, 0.00-0.47); the latter preparation also showed benefit for physician-reported symptom resolution (OR 0.04; 95% CI, 0.00-0.56).
CDC recommends metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days for women and 2 g orally in a single dose for men. Partners need to be treated.

Tinidazole (2g single dose, recommended by CDC) or secnidazole (2g single dose) are alternatives. In an RCT with 131 women, cure rates were significantly higher with single-dose secnidazole (92% and 95%) compared to placebo (1.5% and 1.7%). Treatment-emergent adverse events were VVC and nausea at 2.7% each.
Patients with an IgE-mediated-type hypersensitivity reaction to 5-nitroimidazole antimicrobials should be managed by metronidazole desensitization.

Intravaginal antifungal cream/tablet/suppository (e.g., clotrimazole, butoconazole, econazole, miconazole, tioconazole, and terconazole) for 3 to 7 days or an oral antifungal as a single dose (e.g., fluconazole, itraconazole) are effective in nonpregnant patients. ,, Prophylaxis with lactobacillus products does not prevent post-antibiotic candidiasis.

Non-albicans vulvovaginal candidiasis: The optimal treatment remains unknown. Give a non-flucon azole drug other than fluconazole for 7 to 14 days. For recurrence, give 600 mg of boric acid in a gelatin capsule administered vaginally once daily for 3 weeks.,,

Women with VVC and a debilitating medical condition (e.g., steroid use, uncontrolled diabetes) and pregnancy may need therapy with intravaginal preparations of butoconazole, clotrimazole, miconazole, and tioconazole for 7 to 14 days.,,
Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days; if the patient is penicillin sensitive, give doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days.
Evidence does not support the use of vaginal microbicides for prevention of the sexually-transmitted infections of chlamydia, gonorrhea and trichamoniasis.
All available topical estrogens alleviate vulvovaginal symptoms related to atrophic vaginitis. Other methods of estrogen delivery also relieve the symptoms of atrophic vaginitis.

Best treatment is not yet fully determined; treat based on symptoms, microscopy and culture. Treatment may include: antibiotics- meclocycline 35 mg or 2% clindamycin or kanamycin 100mg vaginally for 6 days, amoxicillin, amoxcillin/clavulinic acid or floroquinalones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacilin, levofloxacilin), steroids, or vaginal estrogen can be used either alone or combined.

ACOG (2020) does not recommend use of probiotics (vaginal or oral) and nonmedical therapies for the treatment or prevention of vaginitis. Lactobacillus when given orally, vaginally, or both had no effect on antibiotic-induced vulvovaginal candidiasis.
Studies have demonstrated that lactobacillus could restore vaginal flora, but clinical outcome data are lacking.

In an RCT of 90 women with both BV and trichomoniasis, addition of the probiotic Gynophilus® 1 capsule vaginally twice daily improved likelihood of cure from TV (88.6% and 42.9% in the probiotic and placebo groups, respectively) and BV (63.6% and 11.9%, respectively) over metronidazole (500 mg twice daily for 7 days) alone, based on TV detection culturally and vaginal microflora with the qPCR-RT and microscopically.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 trials with 1165 patients found astodrimer gel was better than placebo in treating BV with respect to patient symptoms, and clinical (Amsel criteria) and microbiological (Nugent score) measurements.
A small Chinese RCT found that daily vaginal probiotic prophylaxis resulted in lower recurrence rates for BV (15.8% vs. 45.0%).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 10 RCTs including 1656 subjects with CVV concluded that, compared with conventional treatment, the use of probiotics as adjuvant therapy appears to increase short-term clinical and mycological cure and decrease relapse rates at one month but not improve outcomes over the longer term, based on low and very low-quality evidence. Probiotics use did not increase the frequency of adverse events.

In an Italian RCT, a thymol + eugenol vaginal douche given once daily resulted in similar significantly reduced symptoms compared with 1 metronidazole vaginal suppository/night for 1 week for BV or 1 econazole vaginal suppository/night for 3 days for CVV.

1% Satureja khuzestanica vaginal cream administered once daily for 7 days performed as well as 1% clotrimazole vaginal cream for symptom relief and culture results in an RCT of 84 Iranian women with CVV.

A myrtle and oak gall suppository was effective in improving vaginal discharge in an RCT of 120 women with vaginitis due to BV or trichomoniasis. In another RCT of 84 women with BV, oak gall vaginal cream was comparable to metronidazole gel in resolution of symptoms (82.1% vs. 87.5%, respectively).
displays recommendations regarding treatment for recurrent vaginitis.

Recurrent BV has been associated with vaginal cleansing with an adjusted hazard-ratio (aHR) of 1.30. Twice weekly metronidazole gel given for 28 weeks reduced recurrence with absolute risk reduction of 16% (NNT = 6) at 28 weeks follow-up, but the complications of pain and candidiasis surpassed efficacy (NNH = 5).

In a qualitative study of two treatments for recurrent BV, women felt oral metronidazole treated BV effectively and was associated with longer time periods between episodes, but they generally preferred using the lactic acid gel because of ease of use, once daily application and fewer side-effects.

In a case series of 5 women with symptomatic, intractable and recurrent BV, vaginal microbiome transplantation was associated with long-term remission until the end of 5 to 21-month follow-up in 4 of them; remission was defined as marked improvement of symptoms, Amsel criteria, microscopic vaginal fluid appearance and reconstitution of a Lactobacillus-dominated vaginal microbiome.

First treatment failure in a woman re-exposed to an untreated partner, retreat with metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days; if second failure occurs or no re-exposure has occurred, treat with metronidazole OR tinidazole 2g orally daily for 7 days.

Once weekly oral fluconazole (150mg) for 6 months reduces risk of recurrence, but the cost of this regimen is substantial. ACOG (2020) recommends extended antifungal treatment for recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis.
Recurrence following treatment of VVC is 28%, trichomoniasis is up to 20%, and BV is 11%. B

Follow-up and test of cure for most cases of vaginitis are not required if symptoms resolve. About 8% of patients with vaginitis either fail to respond to treatment or have a rapid recurrence of symptoms

Due to high recurrence rates for trichomoniasis (approximately 1 in 5 women), CDC (2021) and ACOG (2020) recommend retesting sexually-active women approximately 3 months post treatment. In addition, the guidelines suggest referral of partners for presumptive therapy and counseling them to refrain from sexual activity until they have completed therapy and are asymptomatic.

BV has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, including premature rupture of membranes, intra-amniotic infection, postpartum endometritis, and preterm birth; data are conflicting about risk of preterm birth.

Antibiotics like metronidazole orally 500mg twice daily for 7 days, metronidazole gel 0.75%, 5g (one full applicator) daily intravaginally for 5 days, clindamycin cream 2% 5g (one full applicator) daily intravaginally for 5 days, or clindamycin orally 300mg twice daily for 7 days are effective in the treatment of BV during pregnancy. However, they do not prevent preterm birth (PTB) before 37 weeks among women with or without previous PTB, even if given prior to 20 weeks of gestation. Authors of a Cochrane review of 21 trials concluded no decreased risk of PTB with treatment. Antibiotic treatment appears to reduce the risk of late miscarriage. Oral antibiotics such as metronidazole or clindamycin have advantages over vaginal antibiotics with respect to neonatal unit admission, prolonged gestational age, and birth weight.

T. vaginalis has been associated with a greater likelihood of preterm birth (OR 1.27; 95% CI, 1.08-1.50), premature rupture of membranes (OR 1.87; 95% CI, 1.53-2.29), and infants of low birth weight (OR 2.12; 95% CI, 1.15-3.91).

Metronidazole, as a single oral dose of 2g, is effective against trichomoniasis in pregnancy, but the effect on pregnancy outcome is uncertain. In a US trial using metronidazole for women between 16 and 23 weeks gestation (dosed on two occasions at least 2 weeks apart), the trial was stopped early because of lack of effect in reducing PTB and a likelihood of harm.

VVC is treated with intravaginal preparations of butoconazole, clotrimazole, miconazole, or tioconazole for 7 to 14 days., A topical imidazole is more effective than nystatin, and an intravaginal antifungal for 7 days has a 90% cure rate in pregnant women.The CDC notes that epidemiologic studies indicate a single 150mg dose of fluconazole might be associated with spontaneous abortion and congenital anomalies and should be avoided.

Vaginitis in the pediatric population most commonly affects prepubertal girls, predominantly due to non-infectious causes (25%-75% with vaginal symptoms), inadequate hygiene, intravaginal foreign body or contact dermatitis.
Common infectious causes are Streptococcus pyogenes (group A beta hemolytic), Haemophilus influenzae, Enterobius vermicularis (pin worms), and least common include candida, yersinia or shigella
Bacterial causes are often associated with an acute and visible discharge; a foul odor or bloody discharge can occur with the presence of a foreign body.
Evaluate vaginal secretions by microscopy and send a sample for culture.
Relying on leukocytes alone for diagnosis of suspected BV in children has a low specificity (59%) and low positive predictive value (53%) for the presence of pathogenic bacteria.
Direct therapy toward the specific culture result in proven BV; most commonly these infections involve Haemophilus influenzae and group A streptococci.

Speculum evaluation is usually not needed; but for concerns of sexual abuse, STIs, blood-stained discharge, suspicion of foreign body, consider sampling vaginal discharge for microbiological study and culture examination under anesthesia - should be considered in cases of or need to identify infecting organism due to suspicion of sexual abuse.

Treat based on severity of symptoms and evaluation: oral amoxicillin 50mg/kg/day, divided into 3 doses for 10 days for confirmed or suspected Streptococcus pyogenes or Haemophilus influenzae infection; amoxicillin-clavulanate for Staphylococcus aureus, amoxicillin-resistant H. influenzae; trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 6mg/kg/day for 3 days for yersinia or shigella infection

History of fever, abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, prior history of sexually transmitted infection?
pH >4.5; Microscopy: Mobile flagellated trichomonads, Exam: strawberry cervix, vulvar erythema, and/or burning/itching?
Intense itching, vulvar edema, thick, white, "cottage cheese" discharge and/or KOH positive for fungal hyphae?
Three of 4 Amsel criteria (thin homogeneous discharge; positive whiff test; clue cells- at least 20% of epithelial cells; pH >4.5)?
Discharge variable, no clear pathogen. Symptoms cyclical, increased length of the bacilli?
If only symptom is discharge, pH normal (4-4.5); whiff test negative; no white cells likely normal discharge. If additional symptoms present, consider treatment for most likely pathogen.
Yes, suspect pelvic inflammatory disease; test and treat appropriately (see Chapter PID).
